tweet: I told you Oudinot with Vandamme, Regnier and Padoue, eighty thousand men, debouches by Luckau and Bayreuth when the armistice breaks, to stand days from Berlin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Austria is against us. That power has 300,000 men under arms, and will send 120,000 men against Dresden, 20,000 against Bavaria, and 50,000 men against the viceroy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Dresden. To Marshal Davout: Austria is against us. That power has 300,000 men under arms, and will send 120,000 men against Dresden, 20,000 against Bavaria, and 50,000 men against the viceroy.
tweet: Austria fields three hundred thousand: one hundred twenty thousand on Dresden, twenty thousand on Bavaria, fifty thousand on my viceroy. Oudinot, Vandamme, Regnier and Padoue debouch eighty thousand by Luckau and Bayreuth for Berlin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have long thought that Caulaincourt and de Narbonne allow themselves to be taken in by the honeyed style. Metternich. The stipulations between the Austrians and the Russians were agreed upon last February, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Armistice ends: diplomacy fails.
tweet: I long thought Caulaincourt and Narbonne Let Metternich's honeyed style dupe them. The Austro-Russian terms were settled last winter, and I am sure the conditions for me were signed then.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall have the heights of Pirna occupied by the Young Guard. The camp of Pirna will therefore be occupied, the right by 40,000 infantry of the Guard, and 8,000 or 10,000 cavalry, the left by your army corps. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Bautzen. To his secretary of state Maret: The camp of Pirna will therefore be occupied, the right by 40,000 infantry of the Guard, and 8,000 or 10,000 cavalry, the left by your army corps.
voice: I shall have the heights of Pirna occupied by the Young Guard
tweet: I have long thought that Caulaincourt and de Narbonne allow themselves to be taken in by the honeyed style of Metternich.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. I see with pleasure that you are in good health. I have been some days at Trianon. I 1 The above anecdotes of the childhood of Louis Napoleon, now Emperor of France, all will read with interest. In subsequent life he has more fully developed the traits here exhibited. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Trianon days amid armistice.
tweet: I received your letter. I see with pleasure that you are in good health. I spent days at Trianon and my health is good. Take care of yourself and write often. I think of you and send my love.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I informed you of my intentions yesterday. The whole army of the enemy presented itself before Dresden yesterday, and Marshal St. Cyr feared that he would be attacked to-day; I am going there. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Kulm mission: cut the allies' rear.
tweet: I told you my plans yesterday. The whole foe appeared before Dresden and St Cyr feared attack; I go there myself. To divert them, debouch at once and fall on their rear today, crushing the division watching you.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Cyr to pursue the enemy. Napoleon wrote to Murat saying that Vandamme had attacked the Prince of Wirtemberg near Hollendorf, and had captured four guns and 1,900 prisoners, all Russians. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Stolpen. To General Comte Vandamme: I informed you of my intentions yesterday.
tweet: I informed you of my intentions yesterday. The whole army of the enemy presented itself before Dresden yesterday, and Marshal St. Cyr feared that he would be attacked today; I am going there.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The allied army, commanded by the Emperor Alexander, has been entirely defeated. I captured 30,000 men, 40 or 50 guns, 30 standards, &c. The enemy abandoned more than 12,000 wounded men in the villages. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: German ally steadied.
tweet: Alexander's host lies utterly beaten. I took thirty thousand men, scores of guns, thirty colours; twelve thousand wounded strew the villages. Vandamme smashed Wurtemberg's Russians and marches on. Austria's new levies melt half-naked and shoeless after days afield.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marshal Macdonald is to-day at Gcerlitz. Should he continue his retrograde movement, it will be necessary for me to march to his assistance. The misfortune which has happened to the first corps is one which could not have been expected. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Murat's loyalty tested.
tweet: Macdonald stands at Gorlitz; should he keep retiring I must aid him. The disaster to the first corps was unforeseeable: Vandamme posted no sentry and kept no reserve.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Nearly all the generals have arrived, and 15,000 men already, so that I think my loss will not exceed from 4,000 to 5,000 men. The misfortune which overtook Vandamme's corps had an immense material and moral effect on the campaign. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, Dresden, 1813-09-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Dresden. To his brother Joseph: Nearly all the generals have arrived, and 15,000 men already, so that I think my loss will not exceed from 4,000 to 5,000 men.
tweet: Macdonald wavers at Gorlitz; must I ride to prop him? Vandamme's ruin beggars belief: no sentry, no reserve, yet the chief, they say, destroyed himself. His men pour back, generals and fifteen thousand with them; I count my loss a few thousand.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write thus to Marshal Ney — 'We have just received news from Marshal Oudinot who deemed fit to venture within two marches of Wittenberg. The result of this rash movement is that the corps of General Tauenstein and a strong body of Cossacks are interfering with the communications of Marshal Macdonald […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Staff work before Leipzig.
tweet: Write Ney: Oudinot rashly ventured near Wittenberg, so Tauentzien and Cossack clouds cut Macdonald's communications. Few have less brains. march to Bayreuth by the sixth; thence three marches from Berlin, our link restored, and the capital can be struck within days.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Prince Poniatowski protects his right. This retreat was not necessary, but it was ordered so as to concentrate our forces." In fact Ney, like Oudinot, was surprised on the line of march, and lost 13,000 men and 43 guns; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Dresden. To his chief of staff Berthier: This retreat was not necessary, but it was ordered so as to concentrate our forces.
tweet: Write thus to Marshal Ney: We have just received news from Marshal Oudinot who deemed fit to venture within two marches of Wittenberg.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Bruno was captured, not by 4,000, but by 400 men, while he was quietly sleeping in the town, with his whole force. As long as the light troops perform their duties so badly accidents will happen. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his chief of staff Berthier: General Bruno was captured, not by 4,000, but by 400 men, while he was quietly sleeping in the town, with his whole force.
tweet: I general bruno was captured, not by 4,000, but by 400 men, while he was quietly sleeping in the town, with his whole force. As long as the light troops perform their duties so badly accidents will happen.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received all your letters, with the exception of that of the 29th, which was intercepted. Marshal St. Cyr is at Dresden, and the King of Naples on the Upper Mulde. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, Dresden, 1813-10-07
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Battle of the Nations; the Empire cracks. To his brother Joseph: Marshal St. Cyr is at Dresden, and the King of Naples on the Upper Mulde.
tweet: I wrote to you this morning at one o'clock. I am starting for Meissen. The whole Silesian army has debouched by Wartenburg; there is no force from Dresden to Gorlitz, nor from Dresden to Berlin. Marshal St. Cyr will remain at Dresden.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have arrived here. The Bavarians and Austrians, 60,000 strong, posted at Hanau, tried to cut me off from France. I gave them a good drubbing, and captured their guns, standards, and 6,000 prisoners. My health was never better. I am going to Mayence. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Leipzig lost: Paris warned.
tweet: I arrived here. Sixty thousand Bavarians and Austrians at Hanau tried to cut me from France. I gave them a drubbing, taking guns, standards and six thousand prisoners. My health never was better; I go to Mayence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We shall therefore have everything to fear without the energy and the power of the nation. " Posterity will say that if great and critical circumstances arose they were not too much for France and for me. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Battle of the Nations; the Empire cracks. To his arch-chancellor Cambacérès: Posterity will say that if great and critical circumstances arose they were not too much for France and for me.
voice: We shall therefore have everything to fear without the energy and the power of the nation
tweet: I have arrived here. The Bavarians and Austrians, 60,000 strong, posted at Hanau, tried to cut me off from France. I gave them a good drubbing, and captured their guns, standards, and 6,000 prisoners. My health was never better. I am going to Mayence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The movement of the English upon Bayonne has opened up a portion of the frontier. I learn that they have already landed a certain quantity of their merchandise near St. Jean-de-Luz. I suppose that you have removed your custom-house line. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Bayonne frontier open; goods landed.
tweet: The English push on Bayonne opened my frontier; they already landed goods near St Jean de Luz. I suppose you moved your customs line; this deserves your attention. Bavaria urges Eugene to desert me as she did herself, but he reported and rejected it. I see Austria's hand.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Give orders that if ever the English arrive at the castle of Marracq (near Bayonne) it be set fire to; also to all the houses which belong to me, so that they may not sleep in my bed. « NAPOLEON." ST. JEAN-DE-LUZ. 283 To M. FOUCHE, at Bologna. "St. Cloud, i$th November, 1813. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Châtillon congress prepared.
tweet: Burn Marracq castle and all my houses there should the English come, so they never sleep in my bed. To Fouche: hasten to Naples and press the king to march to the Po; tell the queen too, and keep the land from Austria's false promises and vile tongue. I doubt him deeply.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If so, have it armed, as well as all the castles along the Swiss frontier. Not that I have any reason to distrust the Swiss, but because in the present state of the Empire it is necessary to arm on all sides. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Battle of the Nations; the Empire cracks. To his war minister Clarke: Not that I have any reason to distrust the Swiss, but because in the present state of the Empire it is necessary to arm on all sides.
voice: Not that I have any reason to distrust the Swiss, but because in the present state of the Empire it is necessary to arm on all sides
tweet: I am not aware if Belfort is in a state of defence. If so, have it armed, as well as all the castles along the Swiss frontier. Not that I have any reason to distrust the Swiss, but because in the present state of the empire it is necessary to arm on all sides.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will hasten to Naples to make the •king feel the necessity of marching on the Po with 25,000 men; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Battle of the Nations; the Empire cracks. To Caulaincourt: I beg that you will hasten to Naples to make the •king feel the necessity of marching on the Po with 25,000 men.
voice: @caulaincourt I beg that you will hasten to Naples to make the •king feel the necessity of marching on the Po with 25,000 men
tweet: Give orders that if ever the English arrive at the castle of Marracq near Bayonne it be set fire to; also to all the houses which belong to me, so that they may not sleep in my bed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This matter deserves your attention.1 The continental blockade was strong in death. […]”
sourceTitle: To Comte De Sussy, St.  Cloud, 1813-11-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Battle of the Nations; the Empire cracks. To Comte De Sussy: This matter deserves your attention.1 The continental blockade was strong in death.
tweet: The movement of the English upon Bayonne has opened up a portion of the frontier. I learn that they have already landed a certain quantity of their merchandise near St. Jean-de-Luz. I suppose that you have removed your custom-house line. This matter deserves your attention.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If we cannot help it we must allow the Pope to be replaced at Rome, but he must recognise the Concordat of 1813 and the arrangements since made in France for the clergy. If Italy is partitioned Tuscany should be given to King Joseph. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To Caulaincourt: If Italy is partitioned Tuscany should be given to King Joseph.
tweet: I consider it doubtful if the allies are acting in good faith, and if England desires peace. For myself I desire it, but solid and honourable. France without her natural limits, without Ostend and Antwerp, would not be on an equal footing with the other states of Europe.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “At Vitry," he wrote to Berthier, " take 200,000 or 300,000 bottles of wine or brandy for the troops and distribute them to-day and to-morrow. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his stepson Eugène, viceroy of Italy: At Vitry, he wrote to Berthier, take 200,000 or 300,000 bottles of wine or brandy for the troops and distribute them to-day and to-morrow.
tweet: You will have seen, by the various documents which have been published, all the efforts made to obtain peace. I have since sent my Minister of Foreign affairs to the enemy's outposts. They put off receiving him and yet they march forward.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the 27th I marched upon St. Dizier, which was occupied by the enemy. I drove them out, captured some guns, killed a few men, and took a few prisoners. I learned here that Blucher with 25,000 men had gone to Brienne, where he arrived to-day. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Paris fortified on paper.
tweet: I marched on St Dizier, held by the foe, and drove them out, taking guns and prisoners. Blucher with twenty-five thousand men reached Brienne today. I cut his communications, occupied Bar, and now pursue him. If he stands we fight at Brienne on the morrow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must leave garrisons in all the places, call in General Sebastiani and your cavalry, march upon. Meuse and manoeuvre on Blucher's right flank in the direction of Namur. " Marshal Marmont will manoeuvre round Metz. Marshals Ney and Victor will guard the passes of the Vosges. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Marshals summoned east.
tweet: Garrison every place; recall Sebastiani and your horse for the Meuse, turning Blucher's right toward Namur. Marmont wheels round Metz; Ney and Victor bar the Vosges; Mortier holds Langres.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think that it will not be suitable for you to wear any foreign decorations. <■ Napoleon." There was some little difficulty about this affair of a ludicrous nature. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his brother Joseph: I think that it will not be suitable for you to wear any foreign decorations.
voice: @joseph I think that it will not be suitable for you to wear any foreign decorations
tweet: I have had it placed in the orders of the palace that you shall henceforth be announced as King Joseph, and the queen as the Queen Julie, with all the honours, and in the manner usual with French princes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bulow, he said, was invading Belgium with 20,000 men (9,000 being English under General Graham). […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To Marshal Macdonald: Bulow, he said, was invading Belgium with 20,000 men (9,000 being English under General Graham).
tweet: Bulow floods Belgium with twenty thousand, nine thousand of them Graham's English. Meet him with all you have. I trust your vigour where others temporize.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall confine myself to glancing at them, being sure that their ensemble will not escape your penetration. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To Prince Metternich: I shall confine myself to glancing at them, being sure that their ensemble will not escape your penetration.
tweet: PRINCE, The delays which have taken place in the negotiations are due neither to France nor to Austria, and yet France and Austria suffer the most from them. The allied armies have already invaded several of our provinces.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “What! six hours after having received the first troops coming from Spain you were not in the field! Six hours' repose was sufficient. I won the action of Nangis with a brigade of dragoons coming from Spain, which, since it left Bayonne, had not unbridled its horses. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Lyons must hold.
tweet: What! Hours after your Spanish drafts arrived, still not afield! Brief rest sufficed me: I won Nangis with dragoons fresh from Spain who never unbridled. You plead your Nismes battalions want clothes and drill, poor excuses!

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “However, we have made between 8,000 and 10,000 prisoners, amongst them five or six generals. We have taken nearly all their artillery, all their baggage, and killed an enormous lot of men. […]”
sourceTitle: To King Joseph, Farm  of  Epine-aux-Bois, 1814-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his brother Joseph: However, we have made between 8,000 and 10,000 prisoners, amongst them five or six generals.
voice: We have taken nearly all their artillery, all their baggage, and killed an enormous lot of men
tweet: Berthier sent you a courier from the field of battle. I have since despatched the young Montesquiou. It is 8 o'clock, and before going to sleep I send you two words to inform you that the affair of yesterday was decisive. The enemy's army of Silesia no longer exists.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The King of Naples will be pardoned for his treason, ■but you will never be pardoned for the reputation and esteem you enjoy. I know not where all this will end, but it is sure our lot will never be fixed as long as it depends on the Emperor. […]”
sourceTitle: To Prince Eugene, ChAteau  de  Surville, 1814-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: I know not where all this will end, but it is sure our lot will never be fixed as long as it depends on the Emperor
tweet: It is necessary that the vice-reine should go to Paris without delay in order to be confined, it being my intention that, under no circumstances, shall she remain in a country occupied by the enemy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The country is in danger, and can be saved by boldness and goodwill alone. Augereau was in command of the army of Lyons, and the Emperor thought that by operating on the rear of the allies, and threatening their communications, he would frighten the Austrians nearly out of their lives. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To Augereau: Augereau was in command of the army of Lyons, and the Emperor thought that by operating on the rear of the allies, and threatening their communications…
tweet: What! Six hours after having received the first troops coming from Spain you were not in the field! Six hours' repose was sufficient. I won the action of Nangis with a brigade of dragoons coming from Spain, which, since it left Bayonne, had not unbridled its horses.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He must march; let him do as I do, and gain honour. The enemy are falling back in all directions, and seem no longer to dream of Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his war minister Clarke: The enemy are falling back in all directions, and seem no longer to dream of Paris.
tweet: I write to Marshal Soult that with his fine troops he ought to beat the Duke of Wellington, but that under present circumstances a little more decision and vigour are necessary.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It seems that the allies have selected the 3rd February for the opening of the Congress at Chatillon; that Lord Cathcart will treat for England with a dozen Englishmen, Stadion for Austria, Humbolt for Prussia, and Razoumosky for Russia. I shall be to-morrow at Troyes. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Six Days open: Paris protected.
tweet: The allies set the Chatillon congress to open within days: Cathcart for London, Stadion for Austria, Humboldt for Prussia, Razoumovsky for Russia. I shall be at Troyes tomorrow. To Caulaincourt: the foe behaves vilely; villagers flee to the woods.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The struggle was a severe one, but when night fell Napoleon had to return with his shattered army to Brienne with a loss of 6,ooo men and 73 guns. Baron Fain says that the Emperor ordered a retreat upon Troyes by the bridge of Lesmont,. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To Caulaincourt: Baron Fain says that the Emperor ordered a retreat upon Troyes by the bridge of Lesmont.
tweet: The report of Prince Schwartzenberg is a piece of folly. There has been no battle. The Old guard was not there; the Young guard was not engaged. A few guns were taken from us by charges of cavalry.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “However, I sacrifice everything to the necessity of covering Paris. In the event of anything unforeseen happening the idea of putting King Louis at the head of Paris seems to me a good one. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his war minister Clarke: In the event of anything unforeseen happening the idea of putting King Louis at the head of Paris seems to me a good one.
voice: In the event of anything unforeseen happening the idea of putting King Louis at the head of Paris seems to me a good one
tweet: I am much surprised that Marshal Suchet should not have despatched the troops which I demanded from Lyons. They ought to have arrived and I hear no more of them. If the marshal has taken upon himself not to execute orders he is very culpable.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am much surprised that Marshal Suchet should not have despatched the troops which I demanded from Lyons. They ought to have arrived and I hear no more of them. If the marshal has taked upon himself not to execute orders he is very culpable. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Troyes headquarters orders.
tweet: I marvel Suchet never sent the Lyons Troops I demanded; they should be here and I hear nothing. If he disobeyed on his own head he is most culpable. To Joseph I wrote: I meant to strike Alexander at Bar and beat him, but false moves spoiled it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If these monkey tricks are continued we shall all be afraid of death. Long ago it was said that priests and doctors render death painful. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his arch-chancellor Cambacérès: If these monkey tricks are continued we shall all be afraid of death.
tweet: I see that instead of sustaining the Empress you discourage her. Why do you lose your head like that? What are these Misereres, and these prayers of forty hours at the chapel? Have people in Paris gone mad?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In four days I have taken from 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, five generals, 600 officers, from 150 to 200 guns, &c. I have lost hardly any one. The cavalry of the enemy is very low. Should fortune continue to favour us, and the enemy be driven across the frontier, we shall be able to preserve Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his stepson Eugène, viceroy of Italy: In four days I have taken from 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, five generals, 600 officers, from 150 to 200 guns, &c.
tweet: I see with pleasure the advantages which you have obtained; if they had been a little more decisive we should have been able to keep Italy. I have destroyed the army of Silesia, composed of Russians and Prussians. I began yesterday to beat Schwartzenberg.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure the advantages which you have obtained; if they had been a little more decisive we should have been able to keep Italy. I have destroyed the army of Silesia, composed of Russians and Prussians. I began yesterday to beat Schwartzenberg. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Italy ordered to hold.
tweet: I note your gains with pleasure; had they been more decisive we could have kept Italy. I crushed the Silesian army and began beating Schwartzenberg. In days I took tens of thousands of prisoners, generals, hundreds of officers and scores of guns.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Greatly incensed at the universal pillage indulged in, Napoleon issued this proclamation:■ — " The Emperor has to express to the army his displeasure at the excesses to which it abandons itself. Such disorders are always hurtful; but they become criminal when committed in our native country. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his brother Joseph: Such disorders are always hurtful; but they become criminal when committed in our native country.
tweet: I have just arrived at Nogent. The enemy after Montereau fell back upon Troyes with the greater portion of their army. They enjoyed great luck, for the frost enabled them to march across country; but for this half their baggage and their artillery would have been captured.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just arrived at Nogent. The enemy after Montereau fell back upon Troyes with the greater portion of their army. They enjoyed great luck, for the frost enabled them to march across country; but for this half their baggage and their artillery would have been captured. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Champaubert won.
tweet: I just reached Nogent. After Montereau the foe fell back on Troyes in bulk; only frost letting them march cross-country saved their baggage and guns. At Montereau, Bray and Nogent they committed unspeakable horrors; Let Paris know. Austria's Emperor never left Troyes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It was only after the most desperate fighting, and with a loss of 6,000 men, fifteen guns, and two colours, that 1 5 Blucher, with his shattered columns, found shelter behind the Marne from Grouchy and his cavalry. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Six Days of genius against invasion. To his brother Joseph: I send you a line to let you know the happy issue of the battle of Vauchamps.
tweet: I send you a line to let you know the happy issue of the battle of Vauchamps.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you a line to let you know the happy issue of the battle of Vauchamps. General Blucher, who was separated from his army, and who had his head-quarters at Vertus, had been joined by Kleist's corps, twentyfour battalions strong, and by a new Russian corps of twelve battalions, or 20,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Montmirail, Château-Thierry: victories wired home.
tweet: I send word of Vauchamps. Blucher, cut off at Vertus, joined Kleist and a fresh Russian corps, twenty thousand men, and marched on Etoges while Marmont fell back.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Due de Bassano (M. Maret) will send you a copy of the proposals of the allies. You will see by them that your sermons are out of place, and that I do not require to be preached to in order to sign an honourable peace if that be possible. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Montereau: bridges burned, enemy thrown.

context: Ligny, Quatre-Bras, Mont-Saint-Jean — and pursuit. To Marshal Davout: My ambition is to see France enjoy all the liberty possible.
voice: My ambition is to see France enjoy all the liberty possible
tweet: My dream is France as free as may be; I say may be, for anarchy always hatches absolute rule. Two hundred guns must crown the gates and works of Paris within days. Tell me when the first naval pieces arrive.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Give orders so that there may be at least 200 guns in position at the different gates and in the works round. Paris by the 12th June. Let me know when the first naval guns will arrive. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: 200 guns at Paris gates and works.
tweet: See two hundred guns in place at the gates and works of Paris by the twelfth, and tell me when the first naval guns arrive. For three months your trust gave me unbounded power; today my wish is for France all the liberty possible, for I know anarchy always breeds absolute rule.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The enthusiasm of the inhabitants of Charleroi and of all the country through which we pass is beyond description”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Ligny, Quatre-Bras, Mont-Saint-Jean — and pursuit. To his brother Joseph: The enthusiasm of the inhabitants of Charleroi and of all the country through which we pass is beyond description.
voice: The enthusiasm of the inhabitants of Charleroi and of all the country through which we pass is beyond description
tweet: I rode from before dawn and now snatch a few hours' rest; at Midnight I ride again. We forced the Sambre at Charleroi, pushed halfway to Namur and Brussels, took fifteen hundred prisoners and six guns, and wiped out four Prussian regiments at little cost to us. I lost few men.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to transfer my imperial head-quarters this evening to Beaumont. To-morrow, the 15th, I shall move to Charleroi, where the Prussian army is; this will give rise to a battle or to the retreat of the enemy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Beaumont headquarters; Charleroi tomorrow. Dateline corrected from content.
tweet: I shift my headquarters to Beaumont tonight; Tomorrow I move on Charleroi against the Prussians, battle or retreat to follow. My Army is splendid, the weather fine, the country well disposed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marengo and Friedland fime 14, 181 j. " Soldiers: This day is the anniversary of Marengo and Friedland, which twice decided the destiny of Europe. Then, as after the battles of Austerlitz and Wagram, we were too generous. We believed in the protestations and oaths of princes to whom we left their thrones. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Are we not still the same men?
tweet: Soldiers, this day joins Marengo and Friedland, which twice fixed Europe's fate. As after Austerlitz and Wagram, we were too generous then, trusting the oaths of princes whose thrones we spared. Today the same foes conspire again; I ask you to show them French arms unchanged.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The bulletin will have acquainted you with what happened yesterday. I am going to transfer my headquarters to Fleurus. We are executing a movement on a large scale. I greatly regret the loss of General Letort. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Fleurus: Letort lost, Sambre forced.
tweet: My bulletin told you yesterday's news. I move my headquarters to Fleurus and launch a wide turning movement. I mourn General Letort deeply. Seize the estates of the Ghent traitors with the king; such treason must pay.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Belgians, the Hanoverians, the soldiers of the Confederation of the Rhine, lament that they are obliged to use their arms in the cause of princes who are the enemies of justice, and the destroyers of the rights of nations. They well know the coalition to be insatiable. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Ligny victory announced.
tweet: Belgians, the Hanoverians and confederation troops grieve to bear arms for princes who are justice's foes and the crushers of nations' rights. They know the coalition as insatiable. I come as your liberator; join your courage to mine.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bellerophon; I am not a prisoner; I am the guest of England. I was, indeed, instigated to come on board by the captain, who told me that he had been directed by his Government to receive me and my suite, and conduct me to England, if agreeable to my wishes. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Guest, not prisoner: the protest.
tweet: Aboard the Bellerophon: I am no prisoner but England's guest. Her captain urged me aboard, saying his government ordered him to receive me and my suite and carry us to England if I wished. I took him at his word and claim the hospitality due.
